facts.text: Mitosis turns one parent cell into two daughter cells that are genetically identical to the parent and to each other, each with the same chromosome number; human body cells have 46 chromosomes, so each daughter cell gets 46. Mitosis is used for growth and repair: the new skin that grows over a scraped knee is made by mitosis. Before mitosis begins, during interphase, the cell copies its DNA, so each chromosome becomes two identical sister chromatids joined at a centromere. Mitosis is like photocopying every page of a recipe book, clipping each page to its copy, then dealing one page from every clipped pair into each of two binders: the pages are chromosomes, the clip is the centromere, and the two binders are the two daughter cells.

In prophase, the first stage of mitosis, the chromosomes condense, coiling up and becoming thick and visible, the nuclear envelope breaks down, and spindle fibers grow from the two opposite poles of the cell. Spindle fibers from opposite poles attach at the centromere, one to each sister chromatid, so the two copies will be pulled in different directions. In metaphase, the spindle fibers line the chromosomes up single file across the middle of the cell, at the metaphase plate, so each pole can receive one chromatid of every chromosome.

In anaphase, the centromere splits, the sister chromatids separate, and the shortening spindle fibers pull each sister chromatid to the opposite pole; once separated, each chromatid counts as its own chromosome. Because each pole receives one copy of every chromosome, the two ends of the cell hold identical complete sets. In telophase, a nuclear envelope forms a new nucleus around each set at the two poles. In cytokinesis, the cytoplasm divides: an animal cell pinches in two in the middle at a cleavage furrow, while a plant cell builds a cell plate. The result is two identical daughter cells.

If one pair of sister chromatids fails to separate in anaphase, called nondisjunction, both copies are pulled to the same pole, so one daughter cell gets an extra chromosome and the other is missing one; the two cells no longer match and may not work properly. That is why a checkpoint at metaphase checks that every chromosome is attached to spindle fibers before anaphase begins. A common mistake is to think mitosis itself copies the DNA: the DNA is copied in interphase, before mitosis begins, and mitosis only separates the copies, so each daughter cell keeps the full chromosome number. Halving the chromosome number happens in meiosis, which makes sex cells and is the next topic.

lesson_markdown:
# How does mitosis make two identical cells?

When you scrape your knee, the new skin that grows over the wound is made by mitosis. Mitosis turns one parent cell into two daughter cells that are genetically identical to the parent and to each other. The core idea: **a cell copies each chromosome, then spindle fibers pull one copy of each to opposite sides before splitting.**

## Think of a recipe book

Picture photocopying every page of a recipe book, clipping each page to its copy, then dealing one page from every clipped pair into each of two binders.

| Recipe book | Cell |
|---|---|
| A page | A chromosome |
| The clip | The centromere |
| The two binders | The two daughter cells |

## Step by step

1. **Copy first.** Before mitosis begins, during interphase, the cell copies its DNA, so each chromosome becomes two identical **sister chromatids** joined at a **centromere**.
2. **Attach (prophase).** The chromosomes coil up and become thick and visible, the nuclear envelope breaks down, and **spindle fibers** grow from the two opposite poles of the cell. Fibers from opposite poles attach at the centromere, one to each sister chromatid, so the two copies will be pulled in different directions.
3. **Line up (metaphase).** The spindle fibers line the chromosomes up single file across the middle of the cell, so each pole can receive one chromatid of every chromosome.

What do you think happens when the fibers start to pull?

4. **Pull apart (anaphase).** The centromere splits, the sister chromatids separate, and the shortening spindle fibers pull each one to the opposite pole, so each pole receives one copy of every chromosome. Once separated, each chromatid counts as its own chromosome.
5. **Rebuild and split (telophase and cytokinesis).** A new nucleus forms around each set at the two poles, then the cytoplasm divides: an animal cell pinches in two at a cleavage furrow, while a plant cell builds a cell plate.

The result is two identical daughter cells. Human body cells have 46 chromosomes, so each daughter cell gets 46.

## When one pair doesn't split

If one pair of sister chromatids fails to separate in anaphase, called nondisjunction, both copies are pulled to the same pole. Then one daughter cell gets an extra chromosome and the other is missing one, so the two cells no longer match and may not work properly. That is why a checkpoint at metaphase checks that every chromosome is attached to spindle fibers before anaphase begins.

## A common mistake

A common mistake is to think mitosis itself copies the DNA. The DNA is copied in interphase, before mitosis begins; mitosis only separates the copies, so each daughter cell keeps the full chromosome number.

## What comes next

Mitosis is used for growth and repair, and each daughter cell keeps the same chromosome number as the parent. Halving the chromosome number happens in meiosis, which makes sex cells and is the next topic.

## Check yourself

Why does each daughter cell end up with the full 46 chromosomes instead of half, even though the parent cell splits in two?

Got a follow-up question about mitosis? Ask away.
